paragraph.text: Voxelith Engine — Design & Implementation Document
1. Vision & goals

Voxelith is a C++20 / Vulkan 1.3 engine in which everything that exists in the world is a small voxel: terrain, buildings, props, characters, debris and even particles. Nothing is a traditional polygon mesh, so every object can be broken, carved, welded or thrown without special cases. The second pillar is gravity as a first-class, composable field: planets, tubes, flipped rooms and point-wells in the style of Super Mario Galaxy, cheap enough to sample for tens of thousands of bodies and millions of particles per frame.

A voxel is 1/16 m (6.25 cm) in the world grid; characters and hand-held props use the same grid or a 1/32 m sub-grid. Everything in the renderer, physics and lighting operates on this one representation.

text.bold: Edits are the common case, not the exception.

paragraph.text: Data structures are chosen for cheap, local mutation first and for rendering second. A single voxel write should cost microseconds, not a chunk remesh.
Levels compose gravity from a handful of field primitives; the solver never special-cases a level.
The visible world lives in GPU memory in the same layout the CPU edits, so rendering, lighting, particles and most collision queries never copy data across the bus.
Fixed 60 Hz physics tick, integer voxel coordinates, seeded randomness. This makes replays, debugging and a future netcode layer possible.

2. Core architecture

The engine is a set of layered modules around one shared world store. Modules below never call modules above; the renderer, physics and particle systems all read the same GPU-resident voxel data and write edits through one edit queue.

3. Voxel world representation
The world is a three-level hierarchy chosen for cheap local edits:

for compression. There is no octree in the hot path; octrees are excellent for static scenes and terrible to mutate a million times per second.

A voxel resolves to a 16-bit material id and an 8-bit state byte. Material ids index a global material table of up to 65,536 entries holding albedo, roughness, metalness, emissive colour and intensity, density, fracture toughness and a sound/particle class. The state byte carries per-voxel damage, wetness or a colour-variation seed, so a brick wall does not need 10 materials to look varied.

Each brick holds a small palette of distinct (material, state) pairs and stores one index per voxel at the smallest bit width that fits (1 bit for a two-material brick, 8 bits for up to 256). An empty brick is not stored at all; a solid single-material brick stores only the one palette entry. Measured on typical outdoor scenes this gives 0.6 to 1.2 bits per voxel against the 3 bytes of the naive layout.

Every brick carries a 64-bit mask with one bit per 2×2×2 sub-cell, and every chunk carries one bit per brick. Ray-marching and collision queries test these masks first and skip empty space in one instruction; this is the single most important optimisation in the engine.

Resident bricks live in one large device buffer (the brick pool, default 1.5 GB) managed as a slab allocator with four size classes matching the four palette bit widths. A per-chunk indirection table maps brick slot → pool offset, so moving or compacting a brick never touches the chunk data on the CPU. Uploads go through a persistently mapped 64 MB staging ring; a frame may upload up to 16 MB of dirty bricks before the uploader starts deferring low-priority edits.

A chunk's full-resolution bricks load within a radius of 200 m of any camera; beyond that only a mip pyramid (one voxel per 2³, 4³, 8³ cells with the majority material) is kept, down to a single colour per chunk at 2 km. Chunks are stored on disk as LZ4-compressed brick runs in 4 MB pages; the save format is the in-memory format, so load is a memcpy plus pointer fix-up. Edits to unloaded chunks are journalled and replayed on load.

4. Rendering

The primary renderer ray-marches the brickmap directly in a compute pass; there is no meshing step. Meshing was rejected because at 6.25 cm voxels a destructible scene produces hundreds of millions of faces and every edit forces a remesh. Ray-marching makes an edit cost exactly the upload of the bricks it touched.
A coarse pre-pass marches one ray per 8×8 pixel tile against chunk occupancy only, producing a conservative depth bound per tile and a list of chunks each tile touches.

The full-resolution pass marches one ray per pixel through the hierarchy: chunk mask → brick mask → 2×2×2 sub-cell mask → voxel. A 3-level DDA with 64-bit mask skipping averages 18 to 30 steps per ray in dense scenes, 6 to 10 outdoors.
Each ray writes a G-buffer: depth, material id, state byte, face normal (6 possibilities, 3 bits) and a 16-bit brick id for reprojection.

Dynamic bodies are rendered in the same pass: a per-frame BVH over body AABBs is built on the GPU, and a ray that enters a body AABB is transformed into body space and marched through the body's own bricks. Up to 4 overlapping bodies per ray are handled before falling back to depth-sorted splatting.

A sparse voxel octree compresses better and traverses faster for static content, but a single voxel edit rebalances the tree. The brickmap's flat tables keep edits O(1) and let the GPU and CPU share the exact same layout. Compression is recovered by palettes (Section 3).

Shading runs as a deferred full-screen compute pass over the G-buffer. Per-pixel material parameters come from the material table; the state byte modulates albedo variation, damage darkening and wetness. Normals are refined beyond the 6 face directions by a 3×3×3 occupancy kernel that bevels edges and softens internal corners, so tiny voxels do not read as a staircase at a distance.

Beyond 200 m the renderer marches the chunk mip pyramid instead of full bricks. The transition is dithered over 20 m so there is no pop. Because the mip stores a majority material per cell, far terrain keeps its colour and silhouette at about 1/64 of the memory. Characters smaller than 2 pixels switch to a splat.

Every pixel stores the brick id and voxel coordinate it hit last frame. If the brick is unchanged (a per-brick dirty epoch is checked) and reprojection lands within half a voxel, the march starts at that voxel instead of the camera; this cuts average steps by roughly 40 % in slow camera motion. Ray-marched depth is exact, so TAA and upscaling (FSR / DLSS inputs) are standard.

Glass, ice and voxel-water materials are marched in a second pass that accumulates up to 4 layers per pixel (depth-peeled inside the DDA). Refraction uses the G-buffer depth of the opaque hit behind it.
Bindless descriptor arrays for the brick pool, material table and GI probe atlas; timeline semaphores between the simulate, prepare and submit stages;

5. Destruction & manipulation
Destruction is three steps that can each be budgeted separately:
(remove voxels),
(find what is no longer supported) and
(turn detached pieces into bodies or particles). The split keeps worst-case cost bounded even when a player levels a building.
Any
can carve: explosions use
with a noisy sphere so blast holes are not perfect balls, tools use

with a material filter (a pickaxe carves stone but not steel), and projectiles carve a capsule along their path. Material toughness in the material table scales the effective radius, so a grenade takes a 2 m bite from brick and a 0.4 m scratch from reinforced concrete.
After carving, the engine must find voxel islands that no longer connect to an anchor (bedrock, or a brick flagged
by the level designer). A full flood fill over a 4 m chunk is 262,144 cells, too slow per edit, so connectivity is cached at brick level:
Each brick keeps a 6-bit
summary: does solid material touch each face.
A chunk keeps a union-find over its 512 bricks, rebuilt only for bricks touched by the edit (typically 10 to 300).

Islands that are fully inside one chunk are resolved immediately. Islands that cross chunk boundaries are queued to a background job that resolves them within 3 ticks; until then they stay static, which the player never notices at 50 ms.
Islands larger than 32³ bricks are never detached as one piece; they are fractured first.

A detached island larger than ~2,000 voxels is split by a cheap Voronoi over 4 to 12 seed points biased toward the carve centre, with the split planes jittered by brick-local noise so pieces look broken rather than sliced. Each piece becomes a
. Pieces smaller than 64 voxels become voxel particles instead (Section 8), which is where most of the visual richness comes from.

A global budget caps 2,000 awake bodies and 100,000 spawned debris particles per second. When exceeded, the smallest pieces are converted to particles and the smallest particles are dropped, oldest first. The player sees a dense cloud either way; the physics cost stays flat.
The inverse operations use the same ops:
stamps a voxel model into the world or a body,
merges two bodies that touch for one tick while a weld tool is active, and

with a negative sign fills instead of cutting. Because bodies and world share one brick layout, a player can pick up a wall chunk, carry it under a different gravity field, and bolt it to a ceiling; it becomes static again by welding and is then lit, collided and rendered as world.
Every applied

is appended to a per-chunk journal with its tick. Saves write the current bricks plus the journal tail since the last full write; loads replay journal entries that arrived for chunks while they were unloaded. The journal also powers undo in the editor and replay in the debugger. Journals are compacted when they exceed the size of the chunk they describe.

Fracture seeds derive from (tick, chunk id, edit id); flood fills iterate bricks in a fixed Morton order; no floating-point values enter the connectivity or fracture paths. Two machines applying the same edit stream produce identical worlds.

wherever fields overlap, and evaluated
wherever a single field dominates, so the common case costs one texture fetch or one dot product.

Each primitive has a transform, a priority, a falloff shell (inner radius full strength, outer radius zero) and a blend mode (
Fields are stored in a bounding-volume list sorted by priority. For a point

are gathered; the highest-priority
field wins, lower fields of equal priority are blended by their falloff weights, and
fields are summed afterwards. Blending direction vectors through the falloff shells is what makes a Galaxy-style jump from one planetoid to another feel smooth rather than snapping at a boundary.

This is the primitive that lets gravity follow destruction. Each chunk maintains a coarse signed distance field at 1 cell per brick (50 cm), updated incrementally from the brick occupancy masks when bricks change; the gradient of that field is the gravity direction. Carve a tunnel into a planetoid and gravity inside the tunnel points toward the tunnel walls, exactly as the player expects. A smoothing radius (default 4 m) stops single-voxel bumps from flipping the up vector.
Where two or more fields overlap, or where a

field is active, the compositor bakes the result into a 3D texture of 1 m cells (RGBA16F: direction × strength in xyz, blend confidence in w) covering the loaded region. Baking is incremental: only cells inside changed shells or near changed bricks are recomputed, on the GPU, at about 2 million cells per millisecond. Everywhere else the volume stores a sentinel that means

The character controller keeps a

that slerps toward the sampled gravity at 720°/s when grounded and 180°/s when airborne, so transitions feel intentional rather than twitchy. Camera up follows the smoothed up with an additional 0.3 s lag. Designers can pin the camera up to a field's own up (for tubes and corridors) via a per-field flag.

Gravity enters the integrator as a per-body acceleration; nothing in the contact solver assumes a global down. Rest detection uses velocity relative to the local gravity direction, and the sleep threshold is scaled by local strength so bodies in weak fields still sleep.

Analytic fields use fixed-point math for the CPU sampler; the baked volume is sampled on the CPU only for debris that has already been promoted to particles, which are not part of the deterministic state.
7. Physics & characters

The physics module is a custom fixed-step (60 Hz) rigid-body solver whose only collision shape is a brickmap. There are no convex hulls, capsules or meshes to keep in sync with the voxels; a body collides as exactly the voxels it is made of, which is what makes destructible objects feel solid.

Dynamic bodies are inserted into a uniform grid of 16 m cells (matching the maximum body size); body-vs-world pairs are found by testing the body AABB against chunk occupancy masks. Sleeping bodies live in a separate list and are only tested when a chunk they overlap is edited.

For a body-vs-world pair, the body's occupied surface voxels (precomputed: voxels with at least one empty neighbour, typically 20 % of the volume) are transformed into world space and tested against the world's 2×2×2 sub-cell masks. Each hit produces a contact at the voxel centre with the world face normal; contacts are clustered per brick to keep the count below 64 per body. Body-vs-body uses the same test with the smaller body's surface voxels against the larger body's masks. All of this is SIMD over 8 voxels and runs on the job system; 2,000 awake bodies with ~150 surface tests each cost about 2 ms across 8 cores.

Sequential impulses with 8 velocity iterations and 2 position iterations, warm-started from the previous tick. Friction and restitution come from the material table of the voxels in contact (the pair's values are combined by geometric mean). Gravity enters as a per-body acceleration from the gravity sampler, so nothing in the solver has a global down. Bodies sleep after 1 s below the local velocity threshold, scaled by local gravity strength.
Computed from the voxel volume using per-material density. For a
under 4³ bricks this is recomputed on every edit; larger bodies update incrementally by subtracting the removed voxels' contribution, which keeps carving a chunk out of a floating ship cheap.

Characters are voxel models (a 1/32 m sub-grid, typically 16 × 48 × 16 voxels for a 1.5 m humanoid) rigged as a small hierarchy of parts: pelvis, torso, head, two arms, two legs. Animation rotates parts about voxel-grid pivots, with each part re-rasterised into the character's brickmap only on frames where its rotation crosses a 15° boundary, so a walk cycle costs a handful of brick uploads per second.

: a kinematic capsule-like probe built from the character's own voxels tests the ground along the local gravity direction with a 1-voxel step tolerance for stairs and a 20-voxel (0.6 m) step-up for ledges when sprinting.
: the smoothed up from Section 6; movement input is projected onto the plane perpendicular to it, so "forward" is always along the surface the player is standing on.
: standing on a moving
inherits its velocity; standing on a rotating one inherits angular velocity about the contact point, so riding a tumbling asteroid or a rolling log works without special code.
: characters are destructible like everything else. A carve that removes limb voxels disables that limb's input; losing the pelvis part kills the character and its remaining voxels become debris.
On death, the part hierarchy becomes a chain of small
instances joined by ball joints. Joints are solved in the same sequential-impulse loop as contacts.
Hinges, sliders and motors are joints between
instances, exposed to Lua. A door is a wall slab plus a hinge; a vehicle is a chassis body, four wheel bodies and four motorised hinges. Destroying the hinge voxels destroys the joint.
Bodies faster than one brick (0.5 m) per tick are substepped up to 4×; projectiles faster than that are raycast against the brickmap instead of simulated as bodies.
8. Voxel particle system

Particles are the engine's main source of visual richness and they are voxels too: every particle is a single cube of one material, lit and shadowed like the world, and able to settle back into the world as a real voxel. The system runs entirely on the GPU and samples the same gravity volume as everything else, so an explosion under a planetoid throws dust
toward the sky and it falls back

One SoA buffer per class (position as int32 voxel coord + uint8 sub-voxel fraction, velocity as fp16, life, material, seed). A compute dispatch per class per frame does: gravity sample → integrate → collide against brick occupancy masks (the same 3-level mask test the renderer uses, so a particle never tunnels through a 1-voxel wall) → write back. Dead particles are compacted with a prefix sum every 4 frames. Emission is through a GPU append buffer fed by CPU emitter commands, so spawning 50,000 particles is one small upload.
When a
or
particle rests for 30 frames, the particle compute shader appends a

request to a GPU edit buffer. The CPU reads this buffer back one frame later and applies the requests through the normal edit queue, so settled particles enter the undo journal and the deterministic world state like any edit. Grains settle with an angle-of-repose rule (a grain will not settle on a cell whose lower neighbour is empty), which makes sand pour into convincing piles and snow drift against walls. The settle rate is capped at 20,000 voxels per frame; excess particles simply keep resting until there is budget.

Particles collide with dynamic bodies through the same body BVH the renderer uses; a particle inside a body AABB is transformed into body space and tested against that body's masks. Particles that hit a body apply a summed impulse to it once per frame, so a sand avalanche can push a crate.

Particles are splatted as cubes in a dedicated pass after the opaque ray-march: each particle writes depth-tested into the G-buffer with its material and a 6-face normal, so it receives the same deferred shading, GI and shadows as the world.
particles instead accumulate into a low-resolution froxel volume (160 × 90 × 64) that is ray-marched for soft, lit smoke; this keeps a million puffs at a fixed cost.
particles inject emissive energy into the GI probes near them, which is how a spray of sparks lights a dark room.

An effect is a small graph of emitters, each with a class, a shape (point, sphere, voxel-surface, body-surface), a rate or burst, and curves for velocity, life and colour over life. Material-driven effects are automatic: carving a material emits
of that material at a rate from the material table, so stone chips, wood splinters and glass shatters without per-object setup. The editor previews effects in-world with the real gravity field.

9. Lighting engine
Lighting is fully dynamic with no baking, because a world that can change anywhere cannot have precomputed light. The design leans on the fact that the world is already a voxel grid: the brickmap
the acceleration structure for shadow rays and GI, so there is no second scene representation to keep in sync with destruction.
: one directional light with a time-of-day curve and a physically based sky.

: any material can emit; a lava floor, a neon sign or a torch is just voxels. There are no point-light objects in v1, which removes a whole class of light-leak and budget problems. Designers who want a lamp place an emissive voxel.
and emissive
inject into the GI probes (Section 8).

Four cascaded shadow maps (2048², covering 8, 32, 128 and 512 m) rendered by ray-marching the brickmap from the light's view in a compute pass, exactly like the primary pass. Because the depth is exact, contact hardening comes free from a 3×3 PCF with a kernel scaled by receiver-occluder distance. Dynamic bodies are included in the same march.

Indirect light is stored in a grid of probes at 1 m spacing covering the 200 m detail radius (about 8 million probes), each holding irradiance as 9 spherical-harmonic coefficients in RGB (fp16, 54 bytes) plus a mean-distance pair for visibility weighting, in the style of DDGI. Probes live inside the brick pool's indirection, so they stream with chunks and are dropped where there is solid rock.

: each frame a budget of 64,000 probes is updated (full grid every ~2 s; probes near edits, the camera and moving emissive sources are prioritised). Each probe traces 48 rays through the brickmap with the mask-skipping DDA; hits read the material's albedo and emissive and the previous frame's probe irradiance at the hit point, which gives multi-bounce light for free over a few frames.

: the deferred shading pass samples the 8 surrounding probes with visibility weighting from the stored mean distances, which stops light leaking through 1-voxel walls, a problem naive voxel cone tracing has.
: a carved brick invalidates the probes within 2 m, which are re-traced the same frame in the light-injection pass, so a new window lets light in on the next frame.

Emissive voxels are found by a per-brick flag set at edit time; the GI probe rays simply read their radiance on hit. For small, bright emitters (a torch of 8 voxels) the 48-ray probe trace would flicker, so bricks with emissive voxels additionally splat their total emission into the nearest 27 probes directly each frame. Particles do the same from the particle buffer.

A 3×3×3 occupancy kernel at the shading point gives a cheap, sharp AO that reads well on tiny voxels; a 16-sample screen-space pass adds medium-range occlusion. Both are modulated by the probe visibility so they do not double-darken.
A Hillaire-style sky LUT drives sun colour and ambient. A froxel volume (the same 160 × 90 × 64 grid as
particles) accumulates fog density from the level, smoke from particles and emissive scattering, then is ray-marched with the shadow cascades for god rays through broken roofs.

Histogram-based auto exposure with designer-set bounds per gravity field (so the inside of a dark planetoid does not pin the exposure for the sunlit outside), ACES tone mapping, and a bloom that responds to emissive voxels so sparks and lava glow.

The combination the engine is tuned for: tiny cubes with bevelled normals, hard sun shadows with soft contact, warm bounce from emissive materials, dust catching light shafts after a collapse. Every element above is chosen so that destruction and gravity changes never produce a lighting artefact: there is nothing precomputed to invalidate.
10. Foliage system
Foliage is voxels like everything else, but it is stored as

rather than as world voxels, because a forest of 500,000 plants would otherwise cost more brick uploads per gust of wind than a building collapse. An instance is cheap to sway, cut, burn and regrow; it only becomes world voxels (a fallen trunk, a stump) when it stops being a plant.

Ground cover is scattered procedurally per brick from a density map painted in the editor plus material rules (grass on soil, moss on north-facing stone, reeds within 1 m of water). Scatter is deterministic from (brick id, rule id, seed), so it is never saved; only designer overrides and runtime damage are stored, as a per-brick 64-bit kill mask. When a brick is edited, its cover is re-scattered on the surviving surface voxels, which is why digging a trench removes the grass with it.

A global wind field (direction, gust noise, local turbulence from explosions and moving bodies) is baked into the same 1 m volume as gravity, in a second RGBA16F texture. Instances bend as a rotation about their root driven by wind, local gravity (grass on a planetoid hangs
from the surface) and a per-instance phase, evaluated in the splat shader. Nothing about wind touches voxel memory.

Ground cover is splatted as cubes in the particle pass (Section 8), so it receives the same shading, GI and shadows; a 2-level LOD drops to a single cube at 40 m and to a ground-tint contribution at 100 m. Canopy clusters are rendered as instanced dynamic bricks through the body BVH, which gives real occlusion and lets light shafts pass through gaps in leaves. Trunks are world voxels and need nothing special.
: any carve or body contact that intersects an instance sets its health; at zero it spawns 1 to 8
particles of its material and sets its kill bit. A scythe sweep through 2,000 tufts is one GPU dispatch and one 8 KB mask upload.
: characters and bodies flatten instances they stand on (a bend override that decays over 20 s), so paths through tall grass appear and fade.
: carving a trunk uses the normal detach logic from Section 5; the canopy instances attached to a detached part ride along as a
child and shed leaves (
particles) on impact. Gravity applies to the fallen tree like any body, so a tree felled on a small planetoid topples around the curve.
: a material flag
plus a per-brick fire state byte drives a cellular fire spread over instances and flammable world voxels, consuming them into ash
and emitting
and
particles and emissive heat into the GI probes. Fire spreads along the local
so it climbs a tree correctly on any planetoid.

: killed cover regrows after a designer-set time (default 10 minutes of play) by clearing kill bits with a noise pattern, so forests heal between visits but a clear-cut field stays bare long enough to matter.
Foliage types are
models with a

part tag, a root pivot, a bend stiffness and a seasonal palette; density maps and rules are painted in the world editor and preview live. Trees are placed by hand or by a scatter rule with minimum spacing.
0.8 ms GPU for sim and splat at 500,000 instances; 48 MB of instance buffers; ground-cover state is 8 bytes per brick in the chunk save.
11. Liquids
Liquids are a

text.bold: cellular-automaton volume solver that lives inside the brickmap

paragraph.text: : a liquid cell is a world voxel whose material is a liquid type and whose state byte is its fill level (0 to 255). There are no particle fluids for bulk water and no separate fluid grid; the same occupancy masks, edits, journal and renderer carry water, lava, oil and acid. The solver is a compute pass over
bricks only, and it flows along the
, so a tank of water on a planetoid wraps around it and a gravity flip pours the lake onto the ceiling.
Type
Viscosity
Interactions
Water
Low
Extinguishes fire, wets voxels (state byte), floats low-density bodies, grows reeds nearby
Lava

Ignites flammables, melts ice into water, cools to stone where it touches water or after 60 s exposed

Each tick, for every active brick, the solver runs a falling-sand style rule set on its 512 cells in 8 sub-steps: a cell first moves fill into the cell

along local gravity (quantised to the dominant axis per brick, with the two minor axes used for diagonal spreading), then equalises with its four side neighbours, then applies a small upward pressure transfer when fill exceeds 255 so sealed containers fill and lifted water finds its level. Flow rate is scaled by viscosity and by local gravity strength. Because every brick knows its gravity axis from the baked volume, a river on a cylindrical world simply runs along the cylinder. Bricks whose cells did not change for 8 ticks go inactive; an edit, a body or a particle touching them reactivates them and their neighbours.

The target is 4,000,000 active cells (≈ 8,000 bricks) per tick in 1.5 ms. A large lake at rest costs nothing; only its shoreline, inflows and whatever the player disturbs is active. Edits that open a path for liquid are the same
records as everything else, so a dam breach is carving the dam, and the water does the rest.

text.bold: Interaction with the rest of the engine

paragraph.text: : buoyancy is computed per submerged voxel from the body's material density against the liquid's, with drag along the local gravity axis; a wooden crate floats, a stone one sinks, a hollow metal hull floats until it is holed. Moving bodies displace liquid by pushing fill into neighbours.
: swimming is a controller mode entered when the pelvis is submerged; lava and acid deal damage per submerged voxel.
particles that land on liquid add fill;
sinks through water at a viscosity-scaled rate and settles below it (sand poured into a pool forms an underwater pile); splashes spawn
and
from cells whose fill changed by more than 128 in one tick.
: water cells adjacent to burning voxels extinguish them; lava ignites them; reeds and moss scatter near water through the foliage rules.
: no special code. Liquids read the baked gravity volume and the per-brick dominant axis; a gravity flip reactivates every liquid brick and the lake falls.
: a liquid cell has no toughness; carving removes it like any voxel, and the solver backfills from neighbours.

Liquid surfaces are extracted in the transparency pass (Section 4) as the top liquid cell per column along the local gravity axis, with the fill level used as a sub-voxel height, so a half-full cell draws a half-height block and a settled surface is flat rather than stepped. The surface shader does screen-space reflection with a fallback to the sky LUT, refraction from the opaque G-buffer, depth-based absorption colour and a small normal ripple driven by neighbouring fill deltas. Lava is opaque and emissive, so it goes through the normal deferred path and lights its surroundings through the GI probes. Underwater, the froxel volume adds scattering and the sun cascades add caustic-like light shafts.

Liquid is world voxels, so saves, journals, undo and replay already cover it. The solver runs on the GPU for speed but is written to be bit-exact against a CPU reference (integer fill, fixed sub-step order, Morton brick order); the nightly determinism test runs both and diffs them.

Designers paint liquid volumes with the normal brush tools using a liquid material, place inflow and drain emitters (which add or remove fill at a rate), and tune viscosity, colour, absorption and reactions in the material table. The debug overlay shows active bricks and per-brick gravity axes.

1.5 ms GPU per tick at 4 M active cells, 192 MB for sparse liquid tiles and active-set tables, plus the surface pass inside the transparency budget. Still open: whether v1 needs a true pressure solve for sealed containers (the current rule is an approximation that leaks slowly).
. Content pipeline & tooling
All tools run inside the engine on the live world, because the editing operations are the same
records the game uses. There is no separate editor build and no bake step; a designer carves a planetoid, sets its gravity and plays it in the same session.
Characters and props are authored in MagicaVoxel (
) or in the in-engine model editor and imported into the engine's

format: palette-compressed bricks, a part hierarchy with pivots, per-part material overrides and optional emissive animation tracks. Import is lossless and takes milliseconds; a 16 × 48 × 16 character is about 6 KB. Materials are matched by palette colour against the material table with a manual override map per model.

The model editor lets an artist tag voxel regions as parts and place pivots on the voxel grid. Animation clips are keyframed part rotations and offsets, authored in-engine or imported from a simple JSON format; there is no skeletal weighting, which keeps the voxel look crisp.
Brush tools (sphere, box, SDF stamp, model stamp), material painting, terrain sculpting with noise layers, and a prefab system where a prefab is a
placed into the world and tracked so it can be re-stamped after edits to the source. Undo uses the edit journal.

Field primitives are placed as gizmos with their shells shown as translucent surfaces; the baked volume can be visualised as a streamline field or as arrows sampled on a grid. A "drop test" spawns 1,000
particles at the cursor and shows their paths for 5 s, which is the fastest way to tune a transition between two planetoids.
Live graph editing of emitters with the particle system running under the real gravity field; a scrub bar replays a burst.

The material table is a CSV in the project with hot reload: id, name, albedo, roughness, metalness, emissive colour and intensity, density, toughness, restitution, friction, particle class and sound class.
Lua 5.4 through sol2 for gameplay, with a hot-reloading script per entity archetype. The API exposes entities,
submission, gravity field creation and retargeting, effect spawning and joint creation. Heavy per-voxel logic is never exposed to scripts; scripts submit ops and the engine executes them.
Frame-graph viewer with per-pass GPU timings and the brick upload bandwidth of the frame.
Brick heat map: colours bricks by edit frequency, palette bit width or GI probe update age.
Physics overlay: contact points, sleep state, per-body gravity vector.
Replay: because the simulation is deterministic, a recorded input and edit stream replays a session bit-for-bit; the replay viewer scrubs the journal and shows the world at any tick.
Crash capture writes the last 600 ticks of the edit stream so a bug report reproduces itself.

CMake, Clang on both platforms, vcpkg for dependencies (Vulkan-Hpp, VMA, glslang, LZ4, sol2, Dear ImGui for tool UI, Tracy for profiling). Unit tests for palettes, masks, connectivity and the gravity compositor; golden-image rendering tests on a fixed scene; a nightly determinism test that replays 10 minutes of recorded play on two machines and diffs the worlds.

. Implementation roadmap
Five phases over about 1

months, each ending in a playable demo that gates the next. Order follows risk: the brickmap and ray-marcher are proven first, since every other system depends on their layout; gravity comes before beauty because it shapes the physics and camera code; tools come last so they wrap stable systems. A team of 6 to 8 (2 rendering, 2 simulation, 1 tools, 1 technical artist, 1 to 2 generalists) is assumed.
Gravity (accented) sits in the middle on purpose: it must be proven before the lighting and particle work is tuned around it, and it cannot start before the brick layout and physics it samples exist.

import. Gate: a static 1 km² scene at 60 fps / 1440p and a 1 M edits/s micro-benchmark on the CPU brick layout.

field with the brick-level SDF, character controller with smoothed up, camera, ragdoll, joints. Gate: a planetoid demo with a jump to a second planet, a gravity-flip room and a crater that rubble rolls into.

Materials and the look are iterated by the technical artist from Phase 1 onward on whatever renders; the determinism test runs nightly from Phase 2 so non-determinism is caught when it is introduced, not at the end.
